nodes.name: Big bluestem
nodes.desc: A tall warm-season grass that dominates the remnant prairie on the loess ridges and feeds many grazers and seed eaters.

nodes.name: Little bluestem
nodes.desc: A shorter bunchgrass that thrives on the dry, steep bluff tops and south-facing slopes of the hills.

nodes.name: Leadplant
nodes.desc: A deep-rooted prairie shrub in the pea family, listed among the hills' characteristic flowering plants and visited by bumble bees.

nodes.name: Common Milkweed
nodes.desc: A prairie wildflower and the host plant for monarch caterpillars; its flowers also feed bees and other pollinators.

nodes.name: Eastern red cedar
nodes.desc: A fire-intolerant evergreen that spreads into prairie where fire is suppressed, shading out grasses; its berries feed birds and mammals.

nodes.name: Monarch butterfly
nodes.desc: Its caterpillars feed only on milkweed, so prairie milkweed patches are a key resource for this migratory butterfly.

nodes.name: Brown-belted Bumble Bee
nodes.desc: A common bumble bee that visits leadplant, milkweed and other prairie flowers for nectar and pollen.

nodes.name: Prairie vole
nodes.desc: A small grass-eating rodent of dry grassy fields, prey for coyotes, hawks, owls, foxes and snakes.

nodes.name: White-tailed deer
nodes.desc: The common large herbivore of the hills, grazing and browsing prairie plants and supplying carrion for scavengers.

nodes.name: American Robin
nodes.desc: A very widely recorded omnivore that eats insects, worms and fruit, and is itself prey for hawks, snakes and raccoons.

nodes.name: Northern short-tailed shrew
nodes.desc: A tiny, voracious insectivore that also takes voles and other small animals; eaten by hawks, coyotes and badgers.

nodes.name: Bullsnake
nodes.desc: A large constrictor of open grassland that eats small mammals such as voles and pocket gophers, plus ground-nesting birds and their eggs.

nodes.name: American badger
nodes.desc: A burrowing carnivore named among the hills' mammals; it digs out small mammals and also scavenges deer carcasses.

nodes.name: Raccoon
nodes.desc: An omnivore of woodland edges that eats fruit such as cedar berries along with birds and other small animals.

nodes.name: Turkey vulture
nodes.desc: A soaring scavenger that cleans up carcasses of deer, coyotes and other animals along the bluffs.

nodes.name: Red-tailed hawk
nodes.desc: A common raptor of the hills, hunting voles, shrews, snakes and birds; many raptors pass along the Missouri River bluffs.

nodes.name: Coyote
nodes.desc: The most widespread large predator here, taking voles, deer, raccoons and many other animals and also eating cedar berries.

nodes.name: Bobcat
nodes.desc: A secretive cat reported to be rebounding in the hills; it hunts rodents, rabbits, deer and raccoons.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Warm-season prairie grasses use the strong summer sun, especially on the dry south-facing slopes.

nodes.name: Rainfall
nodes.desc: Rain feeds the prairie plants; the bare, steep loess slopes drain fast and run dry between storms.

nodes.name: Fire
nodes.desc: Fire keeps trees such as red cedar out of the prairie; with fire suppressed, woodland has crept into the grassland.

nodes.name: Loess soil
nodes.desc: Deep wind-blown silt, over 90 feet thick in places, forms the steep ridges and holds the roots of prairie plants.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi and bacteria break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the loess soil.
